interviewQuestions.question: Why is it called 'naive,' and why does the model still work well despite that assumption being obviously false?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's called "naive" because it assumes every feature is conditionally independent given the class — for spam classification, that means treating "free" and "win" as statistically unrelated once you already know an email is spam, which is obviously false in reality, since those words co-occur constantly in genuine spam emails specifically because they're both markers of the same underlying spam pattern. Modeling the true joint probability of all features together, accounting for every real correlation, would need an exponentially large number of parameters as feature count grows — infeasible beyond a handful of features. The independence assumption collapses that intractable joint probability into a simple product of per-feature probabilities, needing only per-feature statistics, staying tractable regardless of feature count.

The reason it still classifies well despite being technically wrong: classification only requires getting the *ranking* of class scores correct — which class scores highest — not the exact numeric probability values. When features are correlated, ignoring that correlation tends to bias every class's computed score in a similar systematic direction (the same false independence assumption is applied uniformly across all classes being compared), so while the absolute probability values coming out of the naive calculation are generally wrong in magnitude, the *relative* ordering between classes — which is the only thing that actually determines the prediction — usually survives that shared, symmetric bias.

This is exactly why it performs strongly on text classification specifically: words in a document are genuinely correlated with each other, but each individual word still carries real, useful class-specific signal on its own, and the naive assumption's distortion tends to hit every class roughly equally rather than selectively favoring the wrong one.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate the gap between "the independence assumption is false" and "the predictions are therefore wrong" — specifically why ranking survives even when the underlying probability estimates don't.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The independence assumption, and why it's forgivable

interviewQuestions.question: Why does KNN's accuracy degrade in high-dimensional feature spaces, even when each individual feature is genuinely informative?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is the curse of dimensionality, and it's a genuine geometric phenomenon, not a tuning issue you can fix by picking a better distance metric or scaling more carefully. As the number of dimensions grows, the volume of the space grows exponentially, and data points that might feel densely packed in two or three dimensions become increasingly sparse and spread out relative to that exploding volume — with enough dimensions, essentially every pair of points ends up roughly equidistant from each other, because there are so many directions for points to differ along that the specific distance in any one comparison stops meaningfully distinguishing "close" from "far."

Concretely, this means the ratio between the distance to the nearest neighbor and the distance to the farthest point shrinks toward 1 as dimensionality increases — the very notion of "nearest neighbor" that KNN's entire mechanism depends on becomes statistically less meaningful, because the nearest points aren't meaningfully closer than random points anymore. This happens even if every individual feature carries genuine signal, because the problem isn't about signal quality — it's a structural property of how distances behave in high-dimensional volumes, which no amount of correctly-scaled, genuinely-informative features can undo once dimensionality is high enough.

The practical mitigations follow directly from the mechanism: reduce dimensionality before applying KNN — PCA, feature selection, or an embedding that captures the informative structure in far fewer dimensions — so that "nearest" recovers real meaning in the reduced space; or abandon a raw-distance-based method entirely for high-dimensional problems in favor of a model that doesn't rely on distance in the original feature space at all.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the curse of dimensionality as a geometric consequence of exploding volume, not just recite it as an unexplained fact about KNN in high dimensions.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The curse of dimensionality, mechanically

interviewQuestions.question: You're deploying a KNN-based recommendation feature that needs sub-100ms response times against a catalog of 50 million items. What's the actual problem, and how would you solve it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The core problem is that vanilla KNN is a lazy learner — it does no work at training time and instead scans (or naively searches) the entire stored dataset at prediction time, which means a literal brute-force nearest-neighbor search against 50 million items has to compute a distance to every single one of them for every single query. That's computationally infeasible within a 100ms budget at that scale — even a fast per-comparison distance calculation, multiplied by 50 million, blows well past any reasonable latency target, and this cost is paid fresh on every single request since there's no learned model to shortcut it.

The fix is switching from exact brute-force search to approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search, which is exactly the same underlying idea KNN needs, but engineered for exactly this scale problem — an ANN index (structures like FAISS, HNSW, or ScaNN) precomputes a searchable data structure over the catalog offline, so that at query time, finding approximate nearest neighbors is sublinear in catalog size rather than requiring a full scan — trading a small amount of exactness (it might occasionally miss the single truest nearest neighbor) for a massive speedup that makes real-time serving at this scale actually feasible.

Beyond the search algorithm itself, I'd also make sure the underlying feature representation is well-suited to distance-based comparison at this scale — verified scaling/normalization, and potentially a learned embedding (rather than raw features) if the catalog's natural feature space is high-dimensional enough to suffer from the curse of dimensionality, since ANN search still depends on "nearest" being a geometrically meaningful concept in whatever space it's operating over.

**Testing:** whether you correctly diagnose the brute-force lazy-learning bottleneck at scale and know ANN search is the standard production fix, not a smaller k or a faster distance formula.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Scaling KNN-style similarity search to production
